questions.question: In the analogy Bird : Nest :: Bee : ?, what is the correct answer and why?
options: Wax, because bees produce it
Hive, because it names the structure the animal lives in, matching the Bird:Nest relationship
Sting, because it is a body part
Wing, because it is used for flight
questions.rationale: The relationship in Bird:Nest is 'an animal and the structure it lives in.' A bee lives in a hive, which matches that exact relationship — wax, sting, and wing describe something else entirely (a product and body parts).

questions.question: Why is it useful to state an analogy's relationship as a sentence before checking the answer options?
options: It isn't useful — options should be checked by first impression
It lets you test each option against the exact same relationship, rather than a vague sense of 'relatedness'
It only helps with number analogies, not word analogies
Sentences are required by the exam format
questions.rationale: A precise sentence like 'A is the structure B lives in' can be tested directly against each option, whereas a vague sense that something 'seems related' often leads to picking a loosely-associated but incorrect option.

questions.question: In the classification set Apple, Banana, Carrot, Grape, which item is the odd one out and why?
options: Apple, because it starts with a vowel
Banana, because it is yellow
Carrot, because it is a vegetable while the others are fruits
Grape, because it grows in bunches
questions.rationale: Apple, Banana, and Grape are all fruits; Carrot is a vegetable, breaking the shared category of the other three.

questions.question: In the set 121, 144, 169, 200, 225, what structural property identifies the odd one out?
options: 200 is the only even number
200 is the only number not a perfect square (11^2, 12^2, 13^2, 15^2 are, but 200 is not)
200 is the only three-digit number
200 is the only multiple of 10
questions.rationale: 121, 144, 169, and 225 are perfect squares (11^2, 12^2, 13^2, 15^2), while 200 is not a perfect square, making it the structural odd one out.

questions.question: In the analogy Author : Book :: Sculptor : ?, what completes the analogy?
options: Chisel
Statue
Museum
Marble
questions.rationale: The relationship is 'the person who creates the item' — a sculptor creates a Statue, matching how an author creates a book.

questions.question: In the number analogy 6 : 42 :: 9 : ?, where the rule is 'second = first x (first + 1)', what completes it?
questions.rationale: Applying the same rule: 9 x (9 + 1) = 9 x 10 = 90.

questions.question: In the classification set Apple, Banana, Carrot, Grape, which item is the odd one out?
options: Apple
Banana
Carrot
Grape
questions.rationale: Apple, Banana, and Grape are all fruits; Carrot is a vegetable, breaking the shared category.

questions.question: In the classification set 121, 144, 169, 200, 225, which number is the odd one out?
questions.rationale: 121, 144, 169, and 225 are all perfect squares (11^2, 12^2, 13^2, 15^2); 200 is not a perfect square.

questions.question: What is the recommended first step when solving a classification question?
options: Guess the odd one out immediately
Look at all the items together first, guess the shared category, then check each item against it
Only look at the last item
Assume the answer is always the shortest word
questions.rationale: The solving approach recommends first identifying the shared category from the majority of items, then checking each item against that category to find the exception.

questions.question: Why should you refine a classification category if it initially leaves more than one item looking 'odd'?
options: You shouldn't — pick either one
A correct category should leave exactly one item as the exception, so a vague category needs to be made more specific
It means the question has no answer
It means all items are correct
questions.rationale: A properly identified shared category should leave exactly one clear exception — if more than one item seems to fail it, the category needs to be refined until only one item is truly excluded.
